summary: The note describes how local school systems have been developing and standardizing curriculums since September 2023 to prepare students for an unpredictable future. It covers core competencies like critical thinking and digital literacy, collaboration among businesses, universities and parents, technology integration, local customization, and quality oversight by the DEQCB. It stresses that standardization should allow ongoing evolution rather than stagnation.
one_line: Local school districts are developing and standardizing adaptable, technology-rich, locally tailored curriculums since 2023, overseen by a new quality board and designed to keep evolving.
key_facts: Local educational authorities have worked on curriculum development since September 2023, when the most recent push for educational reform took hold.
On October 5, 2023, Dr. Emily Hart said "the jobs of tomorrow will require a different skill set than those of today, making an evolved curriculum essential."
Starting from November 2023, local education boards hosted workshops and seminars to equip teachers for the curriculum changes.
The proposed core competencies added to the standard curriculum are critical thinking, creative problem-solving, and digital literacy.
By March 2024, numerous local school districts had established Curriculum Development Councils, including Adam Nguyen and Dr. Linda Cho.

In the 2023-2024 school year, schools emphasized integrating technology, including interactive digital tools, coding, and basic artificial intelligence concepts alongside subjects like mathematics and literature.
Michael Santos said technology education is about "how to navigate the ethical and societal implications that such technology brings with it."
Micro-research projects led by Professor Mary Ellis and Dr. Raj Patel have examined educational needs in diverse neighborhoods of local districts since late 2023.
The District Education Quality Control Board (DEQCB), established in January 2024, oversees implementation of updated curriculums and ensures they meet agreed-upon standards.
The DEQCB consists of educators, statisticians, and child psychologists such as Dr. John Harper, and values qualitative student feedback and real-world project outcomes over standard testing alone.
Local customization integrates local history, environmental issues, and industry insights so students are globally competitive and locally invested.
The new policies state that standardization does not mean stagnation, calling for regular updates and iterations to the curriculum.
